newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf Arab insurance seen underdeveloped.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arab insurance seen underdeveloped.

text.p: The insurance industry in the Gulf Arab countries is underdeveloped and too weak to face international competition, a leading insurance official said.

Bahrain Insurance Association chairman Nooruddin Nooruddin said despite the high value of industrial concerns insured in the oil-rich states, insurance premiums made up only one percent of GDP compared to five percent in the United States.
"Despite the high value of industrial installations that are insured in the Gulf states, insurance premium as a percentage of GDP is less than one percent compared to five percent in USA.
"The per capital insurance expenditure in the Gulf is still less than $100 per annum compared to an amount that ranges between $1,000 and $2,000 for the Western world," he said.
"...The insurance industry in the GCC countries is very much underdeveloped and has a substantial potential for growth, especially life insurance," he told the Emirates International Forum in Dubai.

"What the Gulf has today is an insurance industry that is not strong enough to play the expected role in the development of the national economies. It is also too fragile to face the expected threats from competing international companies."

In 1994 the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates -- accounted for $1.8 billion of the total $5.2 billion insurance premium written in the Arab world, Nooruddin said.
He said Gulf states need to take steps to ensure the survival of the industry by setting up a Gulf insurance market, unifying insurance regulations and coordinating licensing.

"The integration of the industry in the GCC is the only means to provide the collective resources required to develop our markets and create new investment and development opportunities for insurance companies in the region," he said.
Nooruddin said latest statistics showed there were 116 national and 63 foreign insurance firms in the Gulf at end-1994.
Motor insurance is the largest class with 27.1 percent, property and casualty follow at 26.8 percent and marine aviation has 21.4 percent. Life insurance accounted for only 8.8 percent.
Analysts estimate that some 60 percent of all insurance premiums in the Middle East are expatriated to Western re-insurers.
